full_judgment:
7. Opposite party, No. 1 opposed the prayer for preemption by filing a written objection. Main objection is that during the survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 number of plots was created out of said CS Khatian No. 139 under various khatians on the basis of possession of the persons. As the land measuring 0.63 acre was recorded in a new SA plot No.92 appertaining to first SA Khatian No.76 then 73 in the names of the parents of the preemptor, so, the land of opposite party No. 2 including the transferred land was recorded in separate SA plot No. 54 appertaining to SA khatian No. 48/1. The opposite party No. 2, vendor and others exclusively possessed their respective lands on payment of rents since the record of rights was finally published in 1964. Similarly, all other owners of the rest land of original CS plot No. 139 now exclusively possess their respective land either on the basis of SA record of rights or by subsequent mutations. The preemptor was not a co-sharer in the holding of opposite party No. 2 and, as such, his application was liable to be dismissed. 

 13. Opposing the Rule, Mr. Md Ismail, learned Counsel for the purchaser, opposite party No. 1 submits that the land measuring 3.49 as was recorded as CS plot in 1917-18 in the Cadastral survey was split up in numerous plots under various khatians during the survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in 1964 and the persons including the preemptor have been exclusively possessing their respective land according to such record of rights. The parents of the preemptor were in exclusive possession in their 0.63 acre of land which was recorded as SA plot No. 92 under SA khatian No. 73 Exhibit 'Ka' while opposite party No. 2 was in exclusive possession in plot No. 54 appertaining to SA Khatian No. 4811. The preemptor is therefore not a co-sharer in the land transferred by the kabala Exhibit No. 8. He accordingly, submits that the learned Additional District Judge did not commit any error in affirming the order of the trial Court in disallowing preemption. He also submits that everyone of purchasers of land of said CS plot No. 139 including the parents of the preemptor got their names mutated and in view of provisions of section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the parents of the preemptor ceased to be co-sharer in said land. In support, he cites the decisions in the case of Haladar Dutta vs Abdul Rob Chowdhury, 36 DLR 193 and Md Khairullah vs Haji Nurul Alam Chowdhury, 35 DLR (AD) 338. 

 23. Ratio decidendi in the above decisions is that a decree of the Court in a partition suit brings separation and division in the joint possession and enjoyment of land. But such decree does not ipso facto result in the splitting of holding along with the jama till such subdivision of the holding and distribution of the rents takes place in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act or the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as the case may be. Such division of the land may also be brought about by an amicable partition among the co-sharers in such land. But the main submission of Mr. Islam is that the total area of land in a plot as was plotted in the cadastral survey in 1917-18 must to be taken as an undivided unit. If such land was recorded in the names of more than one person, all such persons and/or their successors-in-interest must be held to be co-sharers in such plot till the land is partitioned by a decree of the Court or by amicable partition among such co-sharers. Even any sub-division of such CS plot and/or the holding to which such plot appertained in subsequent survey, say, under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 will not result in the termination of co-sharer ship in such land and thereby, taking away the right of preemption under section 24 of the Act, 1949. The argument appears to be unique in the sense that it was never argued since the Act came into force in 1949. We are unable to accept such interpretation of the law. 

 25. Secondly, who are the co-sharers in the expression, 'co-sharer in the land'? To find the answer, we need not go far just to refer to the holding, more popularly known as khatian, comprising of such land. The concept of 'co-sharer' cannot be conceived independent of any holding or tenancy. If the holding is recorded in the name of more than one person, then, each of such person or his successor-in-interest is the co-sharer to each other in such land. Such a co-sharer will deem to continue as such co-owner in both holding as well as in land so long the holding will continue to be joint. Contrary to such proposition as argued by Mr Islam that sub-division of such holding will not affect the land in any way appear to be fallacious. Because, after sub-division of the holding and creation of new plots in subsequent survey, or by mutation by the acts of parties, the previous co- owners in the holding and/or the land cannot be deemed to still continue as such co-owners. 

 26. Coming to the facts of this case, we find, on 30-04-53 and 30-07-54 parents of the preemptor purchased 0.63 acre of land. After the survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 their purchased land was recorded as plot No. 92 appertaining to first khatian No. 76 and then, No. 73, Exhibit 'Ka', Accordingly, they possessed since then, and after them, the preemptor has been in possession and enjoying the land on payment of rents in the separate jama. His possession and enjoyment are absolutely independent and exclusive of others. Similarly, the land transferred by opposite party No. 2 to opposite party No. 1 vide sale deed No. 1677 dated 30-06-91 was recorded as SA plot No. 54 appertaining SA khatian No.48/1. In the partition suit, the father of the preemptor as defendant No. 3 along with defendant No. 2 and defendant Nos. 4 to 6 prayed for saham and the preliminary decree dated 15-12-54 has allotted a saham to each of those defendants on the basis of their purchase. Mr Islam told that effecting partition by Advocate Commissioners failed four times. Mr Ismail submitted that chance of any final decree is far remote for the present successors of the original plaintiff have lost all their interest in such a decree. Be that as it may, the final decree that may ultimately be passed will just formalise independent and exclusive possession of present owners. The submission of Mr Islam that even after so many transactions and transfers since the final publication of CS record of rights, and the long and exclusive possession and enjoyment by the present occupiers on the basis of SA record of rights and/or mutation have not yet terminated the original co- sharer ship in CS plot No.139 as recorded in 1917-18 cannot be accepted. 

 27. In view of above decisions, there is no escape from the irresistible conclusion that even if the land in the expression, 'co-sharer in the land' in section 24(1) of the Act, 1949 is not synonymous to a holding but conceiving of such land without reference to the word 'co-sharer' is neither feasible nor possible. And the word 'co-sharer' in the phrase 'co-sharer in the land' is the key to find whether the preemptor is entitled to pre-empt. A final decree passed in a partition suit or amicable partition though separates and divides the land for the purpose of possession but does not ipso Jacto terminate co-ownership in such land till subdivision of the holding and distribution of rents takes place only in accordance with law. Sub-division of a holding and distribution of rents may also take place in a revenue survey subsequent to the cadastral survey with or without the plot or plots divided into different small plots. As stated above, such sub-division may also take place at the instance of one or more of the co-tenants of the holding in accordance with the provisions of section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Such sub-division always terminates the joint tenancy or more precisely co-sharership in the land, no matter whether the land is sub-divided or separated or not and after such sub-division, the old co-owners of the holding in such land cannot be deemed to still continue as co-sharer in the land within the meaning of section 24(1) of the Act, 1949. 

 28. Lastly, it is now well settled by the decision of our Appellate Division that all lands situate within a municipal area must be deemed to be non-agricultural land for the purpose of preemption. We cannot think of the disastrous consequence of the view as Mr Islam submits that the quantum of land as recorded in one plot in the name of more than one person during the cadastral survey in 1917-18 must be deemed to be an independent unit and in the joint ownership of those persons as recorded then till partition by metes and bound-to declare all such land still joint for the purpose of preemption. Such view will definitely go against the public policy as well.
